What changed in this version, and what to know.
Only with your own copy of the game
The port does not come with the game, and we can't give out game files or help anyone find them. Asking for them or sharing them breaks rule 2 of the community Discord and can get you banned.
Ask in Help & Support on forum.bbport.de: start a new topic. Save a report and attach it: it has the log, your settings and this PC's details (no passwords), so a helper sees the cause at once.
eboot.bin is not the clean 1.09 one

Re-uploaded 1.09 updates often have a 60 FPS patch or other changes built into eboot.bin. The port brings its own 60 FPS and patches only the clean file: with a changed one the game runs at 30 FPS, the effect options do nothing, and some patches (Lance McDonald's 60 FPS) crash the gestures menu or the cutscene after Rom.
Use the eboot.bin of an unmodified 1.09 update, in a new, empty folder. Don't use a loose eboot.bin someone shared.
Copy eboot.bin from it into your game folder (Game files > Game folder) and replace the old one. Make sure it is that folder, not another copy of the game.
Right-click eboot.bin > Properties: the clean file is exactly 93,825,704 bytes (93,667,640 if your dump tool wrote it as a plain ELF file).
Mods must not bring their own eboot.bin: the check at the top of this page names any that do.
It is shorter than the clean file: unpacking or copying it stopped early (the log then says "prepare failed: out of bounds").
Put the base game and the 1.09 update into two new, empty folders again.
Check the size: eboot.bin of the update is exactly 93,825,704 bytes (89.4 MB), or 93,667,640 bytes as a plain ELF file.
Copy everything from the update folder into the base game folder and replace the files.
It is neither the original file (a PS4 SELF file) nor a plain ELF file: it is still encrypted, another tool has converted it, or it is not from Bloodborne.

Windows has too little memory for the start

The game reserves about 6 GB at its start (10 GB at 1440p and 4K) in one block, from the RAM and the page file together. When Windows refuses, the game closes at once with code 3 (the log says "cannot create … MiB of guest memory").
Press Win + R, type sysdm.cpl, press Enter.
In the System Properties window that opens: the Advanced tab > Performance: Settings…, there the Advanced tab > Virtual memory: Change…
Tick Automatically manage paging file size for all drives. Still crashing: untick it, select a drive with free space, Custom size: initial 16384, maximum 32768, then Set.
OK, then restart the PC: the change works only after a restart.
Close browsers and other big programs before you press PLAY.
An antivirus blocks the port's files
The launcher rebuilds a few files at every start; an antivirus that scans them at that moment blocks them (the log says PermissionError [WinError 32] or WinError 5).
Start menu > Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Manage settings.
Exclusions > Add or remove exclusions > Add an exclusion > Folder: the port folder (the one with Bloodborne.exe).
Another antivirus (Avast, Norton, …): add the port folder to its exceptions there.
Still there: move the port to a plain folder like C:\Games\BBPort.
The port is in a synced or protected folder
OneDrive (Desktop and Documents often are synced) and Program Files lock or move files while the port writes them.
Move the whole port folder to a plain folder like C:\Games\BBPort and start Bloodborne.exe from there.
The game folder is in a synced folder
OneDrive, Dropbox and Google Drive keep files online only until they are opened, and lock them while they sync: the game then hangs while loading or shows only a black screen.
Move the whole game folder (the one with eboot.bin) to a plain folder like C:\Games\CUSA03173.
Then choose it again (the button below).

The game does not use your graphics card

Windows has the card, but its Vulkan driver does not answer or is too old for the port: the game then runs on the processor's graphics, much slower, or finds no card at all. Usually a driver update went wrong, or one driver was installed over another.
NVIDIA: download the current driver from nvidia.com, start it, choose Custom (Advanced) and tick Perform a clean installation.
AMD: start the current AMD Software (Adrenalin) installer and choose Factory Reset.
Restart the PC after installing it.
Still the same: remove the driver with Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) in Safe Mode, then install it again.
VK_ICD_FILENAMES or VK_DRIVER_FILES in the Windows environment variables: delete them. Vulkan then loads only the drivers they name.
The game needs Vulkan 1.3 and a current driver; an old or crashed driver ends the game with "device lost".
Update the driver: NVIDIA App, AMD Software (Adrenalin) or Intel Driver & Support Assistant.
Restart the PC after installing it.
Overclocked graphics card or memory: try the standard clocks.
Close overlays such as MSI Afterburner and RivaTuner (RTSS): they hook into the graphics driver.
The Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable is missing
AMD's FSR 4 and frame generation files for DirectX 12 need it. Without it Windows cannot load them, and the launcher offers them as unavailable.
Download it from Microsoft (the button below), run it and let it install.

Unpack all of it over this folder and replace the files, or into a new, empty folder.

Click the button below: this installation uses its own mods and cache folders again. The saves folder stays, and with it your characters and achievements.

Steam turns the controller into a mouse and keyboard

With Steam open, its Desktop Layout sends mouse movement and key presses for a controller it manages, on top of the controller itself: the camera turns on its own and buttons do two things. The port ignores that mouse movement while the controller is used; the key presses it cannot tell apart.
Steam: Settings > Controller > Desktop Layout: turn it off, or turn Steam Input off for your type of controller.
Or add Bloodborne.exe to Steam (Add a Non-Steam Game), then its Properties > Controller > Disable Steam Input.

Less input lag: the game starts each frame just in time instead of queuing frames for the display. NVIDIA Reflex on GeForce, AMD Anti-Lag 2 on Radeon (current drivers); other GPUs ignore it. Boost keeps the GPU clocks up. Auto: On + Boost on NVIDIA, off on other GPUs.
Send frames to the GPU in parts

The graphics card starts drawing a frame while the rest of it is still being prepared, so it is finished about 2 ms sooner. Uses a little more CPU. New: turn it off if you see flickering or missing objects.

For a G-Sync or FreeSync display: the display follows the frames of the game, without tearing and without the lag of V-Sync. Uses V-Sync (Presentation is ignored) and keeps the frame rate a little below the refresh rate (117 FPS at 120 Hz, at most 120). Turn on G-Sync/FreeSync in the NVIDIA/AMD control panel; fullscreen works best.
In the background: a place seen for the first time does not stutter while its shaders are compiled; things drawn with them appear a moment later instead. Each is compiled once and kept.
Colour-coded shows at a glance how each value stands; plain keeps the counter quiet.

One box per line of the counter in the top right; also in the in-game menu. Render latency is the time from the game starting a frame to it being shown, which Low latency lowers; frame time is the time between two frames.

Frames made between two of the game's: 60 FPS on screen becomes 120. Needs a display with that refresh rate (120 Hz or more at 60 FPS); it pauses when the display cannot show the extra frames. Adds a little input latency. Menus and movies are not generated. DLSS needs a GeForce RTX 40 or newer, otherwise FSR 3.1 is used.
FSR 3.1 makes one frame (2×); DLSS on a GeForce RTX 50 up to three (4×).
On: no more frames than the display shows (an uncapped game gets fewer generated frames, and the GPU does less). Off: the multiplier as chosen.
